theme: The trumpets; the two witnesses; the kingdom proclaimed
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 9:1-11:19. This is a long and demanding reading with the fifth and sixth trumpets, the little scroll, the two witnesses, and the seventh trumpet. Read it as a story of judgment, witness, and the arrival of the kingdom, and watch for its connection to Daniel, Ezekiel, and Zechariah.
settingTheScene: The trumpets sound a series of judgments that echo the plagues of Egypt, with the first four affecting nature (chapter 8) and the next three, called “woes,” affecting humanity. As with the seals, the trumpets are divided into six, followed by an interlude (10:1-11:14), and then a seventh. The interlude shows the church’s role in this period: John eats a little scroll and the church prophesies as two witnesses. The seventh trumpet brings the announcement that the kingdom has come.
observation: “I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth, and he was given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit” (9:1).
“Did not repent of the works of their hands” (9:20).
“In the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets” (10:7).
“It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter” (10:10).
“And I will grant authority to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth” (11:3).
“But after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet” (11:11).
“The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (11:15).
“The ark of his covenant was seen within his temple” (11:19).
interpretation:
The fifth trumpet brings a star fallen from heaven, given the key to the shaft of the bottomless pit. Smoke rises, and out of the smoke come locusts with power like scorpions. They are told not to harm the grass but only people who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads, torturing them for five months. Their king is the angel of the bottomless pit, Abaddon or Apollyon, the Destroyer. This is a picture of demonic torment let loose on unbelievers, limited in extent and duration. The sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at the Euphrates, with an army of 200 million horsemen whose horses have heads like lions and tails like serpents. A third of mankind is killed. Yet the rest “did not repent of the works of their hands nor give up worshiping demons and idols,” nor repent of murders, sorceries, sexual immorality, or thefts. This is the tragedy of the passage: judgment does not by itself change hearts.

Then comes an interlude. A mighty angel, wrapped in a cloud with a rainbow over his head and a face like the sun, with feet like pillars of fire, stands with one foot on the sea and one on the land, holding a little scroll open in his hand. Seven thunders speak, but John is told to seal up what they said. The angel swears by the Creator that there will be no more delay: “in the days of the trumpet call to be sounded by the seventh angel, the mystery of God would be fulfilled, just as he announced to his servants the prophets.” John is told to eat the little scroll, as Ezekiel did (Ezekiel 3:1-3). “It was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it my stomach was made bitter.” The word of God is sweet to receive and bitter to deliver, because it includes judgment and suffering. He must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.

Chapter 11 begins with John measuring the temple of God and the altar and those who worship there, but not the outer court, which is given over to the nations, who will trample the holy city for forty-two months. The measuring is a picture of God’s protection of his people (the true temple, understood by many as the church) while the world persecutes them. The forty-two months (also 1,260 days or “a time, times, and half a time” from Daniel 7:25) is a symbolic period of limited, intense testing. During this time, God grants authority to “my two witnesses.” They prophesy in sackcloth. They are described as two olive trees and two lampstands (Zechariah 4), with power like Moses and Elijah, to shut the sky and strike the earth with plagues. Interpreters disagree about who they are: two literal prophets in the end times, or, as many hold, the church in its witnessing role, the two representing the legal requirement of two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). When they finish their testimony, the beast from the bottomless pit kills them, and their bodies lie in the street of the great city “where their Lord was crucified,” while the world gloats and exchanges gifts. But “after the three and a half days a breath of life from God entered them, and they stood up on their feet, and great fear fell on those who saw them.” They are called up to heaven in a cloud. The witnessing church may seem defeated, but it will be vindicated.

The seventh trumpet brings loud voices in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” The elders fall on their faces: “We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who is and who was, for you have taken your great power and begun to reign. The nations raged, but your wrath came, and the time for the dead to be judged, and for rewarding your servants.” The tense is almost past: the victory is announced as accomplished. The chapter closes with the opening of God’s temple in heaven and the sight of the ark of his covenant, with flashes of lightning, rumblings, thunder, an earthquake, and heavy hail. The ark signifies God’s covenant faithfulness; he keeps his promises, and the covenant community is secure.
connection: Exodus 7-10 and Joel 1-2 are the background of the plagues and locusts. Ezekiel 2:8-3:3 and Jeremiah 15:16 describe eating the scroll. Daniel 7:25, 8:13-14, and 12:7 give the time periods. Zechariah 4:1-14 describes the two olive trees. Deuteronomy 19:15 requires two witnesses. 1 Kings 17:1 and Exodus 7:17-19 relate to the powers of Elijah and Moses. Psalm 2 is the background of 11:15-18. Luke 21:24 mentions Jerusalem trampled. Ephesians 2:19-22 describes the church as God’s temple. Hebrews 9:4 mentions the ark of the covenant. Matthew 28:19-20 and Acts 1:8 describe the church’s witness.
application:
Think about the sweet and bitter nature of God’s word. What in Scripture is sweet to you, and what is hard to swallow? Receive both.

Consider your role as a witness. Pray that God would give you boldness to speak, even when it is not welcomed.

Read 11:15 aloud as a statement of faith about the future: the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you see of the hardness of the human heart.
Ask him to give you a heart that repents.
Thank him that his judgments are just and the kingdom is his.
